params.text:
Physical and behavioural signs

Victims of modern slavery often show physical and emotional signs of what they are enduring. They may look malnourished, unkempt or exhausted, have untreated injuries, or wear the same worn clothing every day. Emotionally, they may seem frightened, withdrawn, anxious or confused, avoid eye contact, and appear to have been coached in what to say. No single sign proves modern slavery, but a pattern of them is a warning.

  • Physical: injuries, poor health, hunger or a neglected appearance.
  • Emotional: fear, anxiety, withdrawal or distrust.
  • Coached: answers that sound rehearsed or inconsistent.

Signs that someone else is in control

One of the clearest signs of modern slavery is that another person appears to be in control. A victim may be accompanied everywhere by someone who answers all questions for them, holds their money and documents, and will not let them be seen alone. The victim may seem to defer to this person out of fear, and may not be registered with a GP or able to attend appointments without them.

  • Speaking for them: someone else always answers on their behalf.
  • Holding everything: another person keeps their money and papers.
  • Never alone: the person is rarely, if ever, left unaccompanied.

Poor conditions and missing documents

Look, too, at how and where a person lives and works. Victims are often housed in overcrowded, dirty or unsafe accommodation, with many people sleeping in one room, and are transported to and from work in groups at unusual hours. They may have no identity documents at all, because a passport or ID card has been taken from them and is held by someone else as a means of control. A person who cannot produce their own documents, does not know their own address, has no bank account, or hands all their earnings to someone else may well be being exploited.

Reading the whole picture

Because each of these signs can have an innocent explanation, it is the overall picture that matters. Ask yourself whether things add up. Does the person seem afraid of someone who is with them? Are they unusually reluctant to give information about where they live or work? Do they flinch, fall silent, or look to another person before answering simple questions? Trust the sense that something is not right.

You are not diagnosing or investigating when you notice these things — you are gathering the ordinary observations that let a trained safeguarding lead and specialist agencies act. Poor living and working conditions combined with these signs are strong reasons to raise a concern. Keep noticing, note what you see, and pass it on through your safeguarding route; your instinct that a person is being controlled or harmed is worth reporting, even if you cannot yet explain why.

params.alt: A care worker looking concerned, beside the heading “Physical and behavioural signs”. Key points: Physical; Emotional; Coached.

params.question: Which of these is most likely to suggest that someone could be a victim of modern slavery?

answers.text: Several signs together — fearfulness, untreated injuries, rehearsed answers and reluctance to give information.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: Correct. It is the overall pattern of signs, rather than any single one, that should raise your concern.

answers.text: A single bruise in a person who has clearly explained a recent accidental fall.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: No — one sign with a clear explanation is not, on its own, a strong indicator.

answers.text: A person who talks openly and freely about their home and their work.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: No — being open and free to speak points away from exploitation.

answers.text: Someone who is simply having a quiet or tired day but seems otherwise settled.

tipsAndFeedback.chosenFeedback: No — a quiet day on its own is not a warning sign; look for a pattern.

params.question: It can be a warning sign of modern slavery when someone else insists on speaking for a person and holds their identity documents.

l10n.wrongAnswerMessage: Not quite. Someone else speaking for a person and keeping their documents is a recognised sign of control that should be reported.
l10n.correctAnswerMessage: Correct. Another person controlling communication and holding someone’s documents is a recognised warning sign that should be reported.
